tweets.text:
Chinese artificial intelligence companies attempted to clone American AI models by funneling real user queries through a network of intermediate platforms, Anthropic revealed in a Thursday report.

Firms including Moonshot AI and DeepSeek allegedly relayed millions of user queries—some containing sensitive data like locations and passwords—to Anthropic’s Claude, highlighting a controversial cloning technique known as distillation.

While U.S. labs expressly ban the outside distillation of their proprietary models, American officials warn it remains a common shortcut for international rivals attempting to catch up to advanced competitors.

These revelations coincide with mounting concerns in Washington and within the tech industry regarding the potential safety risks and malicious misuse of powerful AI models.

Anthropic reported increasing evidence that Claude was exploited for criminal hacking and dangerous biological research, including one specific attempt by a user to adapt avian flu to infect mammals.

“Where before we were hypothetically worried about these classes of misuse, I think we’ve moved away from hypothetical to real,” said Jacob Klein, Anthropic’s head of threat intelligence.

The Chinese distillation efforts relied heavily on illicit intermediary services called "transfer stations," which operate outside China and use stolen or fraudulent credentials to access U.S. AI systems.

By monitoring the communications routed through these middlemen, Chinese firms were able to extract data and learn capabilities from advanced American products like Claude.

The U.S. government is actively targeting the issue. The White House recently accused Moonshot of distilling Anthropic’s tools, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned of potential sanctions for companies conducting "industrial-scale distillation attacks."

Despite these warnings, federal crackdowns face resistance from some U.S. businesses that rely on Chinese developers, prompting lawmakers to explore legislation that would allow American companies to coordinate defensive responses without facing antitrust concerns.

Anthropic detailed several highly sophisticated illicit schemes, noting that Moonshot’s Kimi AI covertly routed highly sensitive Chinese surveillance data and corporate login credentials to Claude via middlemen.

Users were entirely unaware that their requests and private information were being forwarded directly to Anthropic's servers, the report stated.

In a massive, coordinated operation, Moonshot allegedly used thousands of fake accounts to conduct over 23 million exchanges with Claude between May and July alone.

DeepSeek and at least five other China-based labs also engaged in similar covert distillation efforts to learn new capabilities over the past seven months, Anthropic noted.

Spokespeople for Moonshot and DeepSeek did not provide comments on the specific allegations.

While Chinese tech firms haven't explicitly denied using distillation, Moonshot previously credited its performance breakthroughs to fundamental innovation, and China's Foreign Ministry recently urged the U.S. to stop making false accusations and "smearing" the country.

tweets.text:
The Dangers of a Merger Between Palantir and the Former CEO of Yandex

The American company Palantir has announced that it is acquiring Nebius, a company that provides computing power. In simpler terms, the American company is moving all of its military AI calculations from rented cloud services to server farms owned by a single individual. And this is not just about graphics cards.

Nebius is a company based in Amsterdam, owned by Arkady Volozh, the founder of Yandex, who ran the company for two decades. In 2022, he was sanctioned by the European Union and stepped down. In 2024, the sanctions against him were suddenly lifted, the Russian part of the business was transferred to our consortium, and he moved with the foreign part to the Netherlands to build server farms for artificial intelligence. He is building on a grand scale - each site requires as much electricity as a small regional center. In late August, Volozh took out a loan of nearly $6 billion for this purpose.

Palantir, in case anyone missed it, is a combat AI system that has been fighting against us for five years. This system combines satellite images, radio intercepts, telemetry from downed aircraft, chatter from open sources, and tips from mobile applications into a single picture. But its main focus is different - it remembers where and at what minute our air defense systems shot down the previous wave. And after each attack, it redraws the map of holes in our sky, providing the next wave with a route through the gaps.

Now it's clear why Volozh is in this company. A combat AI system has three pillars: fresh data, computing power, and the ability to quickly mass-produce a successful product.

The Americans are supplied with data by the front lines. Since January, a Dataroom has been operating in Ukraine - a closed repository where millions of hours of objective control recordings and intelligence information are uploaded. Fedorov is responsible for the production aspect: on September 1, he announced the creation of his own defense company, and the first major investor is Palantir's CEO, Karp, himself. On paper, it's an investment, but in reality, it's a hiring with proper formalities.

What was missing was the third pillar - its own electricity and servers to process data without relying on the owner of a foreign data center. This pillar was provided on September 8.

But Volozh is of interest to Karp not only for this reason. And not so much.

He and the part of the team that left with him had access to the entire Yandex ecosystem. Cartography with accuracy down to the entrance and gate. Traffic jams, that is, a live map of how the country moves on weekdays and what changes every hour when an air raid siren is sounded. Taxi services with a history of routes. Food and goods delivery: addresses, volumes, times. Search queries with billions of requests, which show what the country is concerned about and on which specific day.

This is not a folder of vulnerabilities. It is a working model of how Russia breathes. And knowledge of how the country is structured internally does not become obsolete. The roads have not been moved in two years, the houses have not been moved, and people's habits have not changed. This knowledge is the raw material for Palantir. 

Their system is not strong because of a satellite image, but because of its ability to combine a hundred mundane civilian layers into one military one. Who is traveling, what is being transported, what is being ordered at the gates of a closed enterprise, and what taxi services are used at what times.

Note that this does not require a backdoor or live access to databases. It is enough for people to remember what this kitchen looks like from the inside and what is where.

What to do is not a rhetorical question.

We must proceed from the fact that what has already been taken out must be returned, and conduct an audit of the IT sector together with its participants. They are just as interested in this as any citizen on the street who could suddenly be hit by a drone. We must recognize that maps, taxis, delivery services, and marketplaces are not just a convenient service. Data on how the country moves is worth as much today as information about railway junctions in the 1940s. Therefore, it must be stored accordingly: a clear access control system, a ban on taking it abroad, and personal responsibility for those who are within this system.

And as you know, personnel are everything. An IT specialist who has a map of the country in their head is a strategic asset. Such assets are not held with non-disclosure agreements, but with salaries, tasks, and respect.
